The purposes of these rites were to honour the deceased, to plead for divine favour, and to console the bereaved. Among the diverse customs that developed, funeral oratory emerged as a favourite means of responding to death, for it could, more than any other activity, highlight the personal characteristics of the deceased, while serving as a means of reinforcing social bonds. The Roman chronicler Polybius described some of the benefits of a typical funeral, arguing that such ceremonies and celebrations invoked pride and inspired others to emulate the behaviour and deeds of the deceased. The tone of orations was positive. Families kept these eulogies as reminders and enduring obituaries, that acted as a kind of moral heritage. Sermons stressed that grief was natural but should be controlled, and that the bereaved should present a brave face to the world, easing the suffering of others. Indeed, funeral sermons often argued that grief should be rational, having an appropriate level of grief. Over the course of the twentieth century, the orators, unlike their predecessors, often recalled the foibles of the deceased, as well as their finer moments. The Athenian leader Pericles, as reported by Thucydides, said: I should have preferred that men's deeds be honoured in deed only, and, with such an honour as this public funeral, which you are now witnessing.
